title: Lesson 86: Capstone III: Evaluate, Harden, Deploy, Monitor
description: Growing the three-tier eval suite from production failures and gating releases on it, hardening against the excessive agency root causes of functionality, permissions and autonomy, staged canary rollout governed by an error budget, instrumenting agent traces and dashboards with named alerts, and the incident path with its postmortem ratio.

questions.question: Three weeks after stage 1 opened, the human edit rate on drafted returns has risen from 12 percent to 24 percent. Complaint volume and customer satisfaction are unchanged, and nobody has rerun the golden set. What does the lesson say is happening?
options: Nothing actionable, because quality problems should be judged by customer satisfaction rather than by internal edit metrics
A rising edit rate with a flat complaint rate is a system telling you it got worse and nobody outside the team has noticed yet.
The edit rate threshold is set too low, so the fix is to raise it to 30 percent to match the regional baseline
The retrieval index has drifted, so the only reliable response is to rebuild the index from scratch
questions.explanation: The lesson names edit rate as the metric to watch in stages 1 through 3 and the one teams forget to instrument, because it moves within days of a retrieval or prompt regression, well before complaint rates move. The prescribed reading is a quality review of the top ten edits rather than a threshold adjustment, and the same signal measured against the fixed golden set of 40 cases is the comparable weekly number.

questions.question: A severity 3 quality incident on one case class is closed with six prompt edits and no new test coverage. Per the lesson, what is wrong with the closure?
options: The incident should have been escalated to severity 2, since any quality drop after launch is customer facing
Prompt edits are held in a console rather than version control, so the closure cannot be audited
Nothing, because a prompt edit is faster to apply than a code change and the incident is closed with an owner
Every postmortem produces at least one new eval case and at most one prompt change.
questions.explanation: The lesson gives the postmortem ratio directly, and it explains why the ratio matters: a team that answers every incident with a prompt edit accumulates an unreadable instruction set and no test coverage, so the same incident returns in a different disguise. At most one prompt change keeps the instruction set comprehensible, and at least one eval case converts the incident into a regression test.

questions.question: The error budget burns 40 percent of its monthly allowance in two days. A product owner argues for shipping the prompt improvement immediately, on the grounds that it will fix the problem faster than any other option. What does the lesson say the team should do?
options: Sixty cases a month is not much, and when the budget burns down the response is to stop shipping changes rather than to ship faster to fix things.
Spend the remaining budget on the fix, because an error budget exists precisely to fund corrective changes
Move the rollout back a stage for one week and then resume shipping at the same rate
Raise the availability objective to 99.9 percent so the burn no longer breaches the documented threshold
questions.explanation: The lesson treats the availability objective of 99.5 percent as a budget to spend rather than a target to hit, and states the consequence of a burn in those words. Raising an objective to escape a burn defeats the purpose, and the SRE material it cites notes that an objective which reflects what users care about should drive prioritization.
